overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Mechanics of Miscounting
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 60a–60b
overview.hebrewSource: יָצְאוּ שְׁנַיִם כְּאַחַת — מוֹנֶה אוֹתָם שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by resolving an apparent contradiction between two baraitot about nineteen lambs, through Rav Huna bar Seḥora's clever reading of a two-gated pen — a solution Rava himself praises. A new mishna then details what happens when two animals emerge simultaneously (counted as a pair) or when the owner misnames animals near the tenth position: calling the ninth 'tenth,' the tenth 'ninth,' and the eleventh 'tenth' sanctifies all three with different statuses, a ruling Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda debate in terms of substitution law. The Gemara explores whether Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule — that the tenth is sanctified 'according to his number' when counting by pairs or hundreds — refers to the owner's own count or the animals' actual count, and closes by examining what happens when two animals emerge at the exact same moment, testing whether 'removing the name of the tenth' is truly required in every case.

slides.title: 🔢 Resolving the Nineteen-Lambs Puzzle
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot seem to contradict — Rav Huna bar Seḥora's answer

nodes.content: ❓ One baraita: 19 lambs → remainder combines forward. Another: 19 lambs → remainder is simply exempt. Contradiction!
🚪 Rav Huna bar Seḥora: the second baraita involves a pen with TWO openings — 9 exit each side, and the 19th (remaining) animal is fit to exit either way
🔟 So all 19 (not just 10) are part of one 'fit to reach ten' count on EACH side — hence total exemption, not partial combination
🎉 Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: 'Blessed is the mother of Rav Huna bar Seḥora' — he matched Rava's own halakha exactly, unprompted

slides.title: 😵 Three Animals, Three Different Statuses
slides.subtitle: The mishna's core scenario of consecutive misnaming
rows: Eaten only once blemished — not fully sacred
Full animal-tithe status — sanctified regardless of the naming error
Sacrificed as a peace offering, per Rabbi Meir; disputed by Rabbi Yehuda

callout.label: The governing principle:
callout.text: As long as the name 'tenth' is eventually removed from the true tenth animal (by mistakenly calling it 'ninth'), the eleventh can pick up the misapplied 'tenth' designation and become sanctified too.

slides.title: 🔁 Substitute of a Substitute?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on the eleventh animal's status

lines.speaker: R' Meir
lines.text: The eleventh, mistakenly called 'tenth,' is sacrificed as a peace offering — like an ordinary substitute for tithe.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: But can a substitute (the tenth already has that role) itself generate ANOTHER substitute? That shouldn't be possible!

lines.speaker: R' Meir's camp responds
lines.text: If the eleventh were truly a 'substitute of a substitute,' it wouldn't be sacrificed at all — the fact that it IS sacrificed proves it's not viewed that way.

lines.speaker: Bottom line
lines.text: The mishna's principle stands: 'as long as the name of the tenth is not removed, the eleventh cannot become sacred' — R' Yehuda's substitute framing doesn't override this.

slides.title: 🔁 Whose Count Is It — His, or the Animals'?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule tested against the mishna's own language

boxes.title: Rav Mari: 'His Own Count'
items: If counting by pairs, the pair he CALLS 'ten' is sanctified — regardless of actual animal number
Fits the mishna: calling the 10th 'ninth' and 11th 'tenth' creates flawed status, since the DESIGNATION shifted

boxes.title: Rav Kahana: 'Animal Count'
items: The animal that is numerically the tenth is sanctified, regardless of what the owner calls it
Reconciled by R' Yoḥanan: this applies only when animals emerge naturally one by one, not when the owner planned to count in pairs from the start

slides.title: ⚖️ Two Emerge Together — Does 'Removing the Name' Still Apply?
slides.subtitle: Rava's rulings on simultaneous emergence

steps.content: 1️⃣ Two animals emerge together AS THE NINTH, both called 'ninth': the true tenth (whichever one it is) is sacred; the actual ninth is not — but since they're mixed up, BOTH graze until blemished
2️⃣ Two emerge together AS THE TENTH, both called 'tenth': tenth and eleventh are intermingled — since he called them BOTH 'tenth' simultaneously

3️⃣ Rav Ashi's challenge to Rav Kahana: doesn't this violate the rule that the true tenth's name must be 'removed' first? Rav Kahana: that rule applies only when they emerge ONE AFTER THE OTHER, not simultaneously
4️⃣ When two emerge as one, BOTH become sanctified together — a special case outside the general naming-removal principle

summary.principle: Tithe status tracks a genuine sequential count, but errors near the tenth position create cascading, partial sanctities — and simultaneous emergence of two animals is governed by its own distinct rule rather than the usual name-removal requirement.

flowSteps.content: 🔢 Rav Huna bar Seḥora resolves the 19-lambs contradiction via a two-gated pen where all 19 are 'fit to ten'
😵 Consecutive misnaming near the tenth creates three different statuses: blemish-only, full tithe, peace offering

columns.content: 🔁 Rav Mari (owner's designation) vs. Rav Kahana (actual animal number) dispute whose count controls
⚖️ Simultaneous emergence sanctifies both animals together, bypassing the usual 'name removal' rule

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the tenth's sanctity, and any cascading errors around it, depend on precise sequence and genuine intent, not mechanical labeling alone

quiz.q: How does Rav Huna bar Seḥora resolve the apparent contradiction between two baraitot about nineteen lambs?
o: He says one baraita is simply incorrect
He explains the second baraita involves a pen with two openings, where nine exit each side and the last remaining lamb is 'fit' to exit either way, creating total exemption for all nineteen
He claims lambs and sheep are treated differently
He says the contradiction cannot be resolved
quiz.e: Rav Huna bar Seḥora interprets the second baraita as describing a two-gated pen where the structure of the exits makes all nineteen animals part of a 'fit to reach ten' count on each side, explaining the total exemption rather than partial combination.

quiz.q: In the mishna's scenario where the owner mistakenly calls the 9th 'tenth,' the 10th 'ninth,' and the 11th 'tenth,' what is the halakhic status of the 11th animal according to Rabbi Meir?
o: It has no sanctity at all
It is sacrificed as a peace offering
It must be left to die
It becomes the new animal tithe, replacing the 10th
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir rules that since the true tenth's name was 'removed' by mistakenly calling it 'ninth,' the eleventh (mistakenly called 'tenth') picks up sanctity and is sacrificed as a peace offering.

quiz.q: What is Rabbi Yehuda's objection to sacrificing the eleventh animal as a peace offering in this scenario?
o: He believes the eleventh animal has no value
He questions whether a substitute (the type of status the eleventh would carry) can itself generate another substitute
He says only priests may raise this objection
He agrees completely with Rabbi Meir
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda challenges whether a 'substitute of a substitute' is even a valid halakhic category — since the tenth (or its substitute) already occupies that role, can the eleventh become yet another layer of substitution?

quiz.q: According to Rav Mari's understanding of Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule, if someone counts animals in pairs (calling the first pair 'one,' second pair 'two,' etc.), which animal is sanctified as the tithe?
o: The actual tenth animal by physical count, regardless of naming
Whichever pair the owner explicitly designates as 'ten' — i.e., animals 19 and 20
The first animal that exits
None of the animals are sanctified in this scenario
quiz.e: Rav Mari holds that sanctity follows the owner's own designated count — so if he calls the fifth pair 'ten,' that pair (the 19th and 20th animals) receives the tithe sanctity, not necessarily the physically tenth animal.

quiz.q: According to Rav Kahana, why does the normal rule requiring the 'name of the tenth' to be removed before an eleventh animal can gain sanctity NOT apply when two animals emerge from the pen simultaneously?
o: Because simultaneous emergence never has any halakhic significance
That rule applies only when animals emerge one after another in sequence; when two emerge together and are both called 'tenth,' both become sanctified together as a special case
Because animals that emerge together are always non-sacred
Because the Torah only discusses animals emerging one at a time
quiz.e: Rav Kahana explains to Rav Ashi that the requirement to 'remove the name of the tenth' before an eleventh can gain sanctity applies specifically to sequential emergence; when two animals emerge simultaneously and are named together, they are both sanctified as an exception to that rule.
